newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon to buy Texas Instruments unit.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon to buy Texas Instruments unit.

text.p: Raytheon Co. said Monday it has agreed to buy Texas Instruments Inc.'s missile and defence business for $2.95 billion in cash, raising speculation that it will bolster its defence operations through further acquisitions.

The buyout -- Raytheon's third in the past two years -- strengthens the company's leadership in defence electronics as it seeks to grow further in an industry that has been consolidating in the years since the end of the Cold War.
The deal was not expected to result in any job cuts, the companies said.

The deal, welcomed by Wall Street analysts, is expected to increase Raytheon's annualized defence electronics sales to $8 billion and its current defence electronics backlog to $9.3 billion, boosting total annualized revenues to about $15 billion.

"We have consistently said that we intend to remain a top-tier player in the defence business and that we see defence as an area of growth for us," Raytheon Chief Financial Officer Peter D'Angelo told reporters in a telephone conference call.

Both Raytheon and Texas Instrument's Defence Systems & Electronics Group, to be renamed Raytheon TI Systems, manufacture missiles, sensors and seekers and aircraft and ground radar, but do not overlap, analysts said.

TI Systems has about 12,000 employees and is expected to have 1996 revenues of about $1.8 billion. Its products include the High-Speed Anti-Radiation Missile (HARM) and the Paveway laser-guided weapons programme, which were heavily used by coalition forces in the Gulf War.

Raytheon is a leader in air-to-air and ship-defence missiles, ground-based and shipboard radar, and has a major but weakening presence in missile defence systems such as the Patriot programme, which gained fame in the Gulf War.

TI Systems President David Welp, who will continue to head the Raytheon unit, said the recent merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. and other mergers in the industry forced Texas Instruments to sell.
"There's been a growing concern about our ability to compete and win alone. We needed to be joined with somebody so that we could have a larger critical mass," Welp said in the conference call.

Texas Instruments Chairman Jim Adams told Reuters the sale would allow his company to focus on the high-margin market for digital signal processing chips, which translate speech, sound waves and other data into a computer-readable format.
Raytheon said the acquisition is not expected to affect earnings per share this year and should provide increasingly positive contributions to earnings per share thereafter.

The deal would raise the Lexington, Mass.-based company's total debt to more than $6.6 billion. Debt-rating service Moody's Investors Service Inc. said it placed all Raytheon bonds under review for a possible downgrade.
The sale has been approved by the boards of both companies, and is expected to close in 1997's second quarter, subject to government antitrust review.
Raytheon's D'Angelo said goodwill tax credits will probably cut about about $550 million from the cost of TI Systems, for a total cost of about $2.4 billion.
Still, some analysts said the price may be too high.
"It's a full price. Even $2.4 billion probably still sets the high-water mark," said Jack Modzelewski, an analyst with Paine Webber.
Raytheon likely paid the high price to give it a step up in the expected bidding for General Motors Corp.'s Hughes Electronics Corp., analysts said.

Raytheon probably paid the hefty amount so it could conduct a cash rather than a stock deal, which would complicate a Raytheon stock bid for Hughes, analysts said. The Raytheon spokesman declined to say if Raytheon was a suitor for Hughes.

Northrop Grumman Corp. is expected to be Raytheon's other major competitor in the bidding for Hughes, most analaysts said. Peter Aseritis, an analyst with investment bank CS First Boston, said Lockheed Martin Corp. may enter the bidding for Hughes, but most analysts said antitrust issues would keep the giant on the sidelines.
"They (Raytheon and Hughes) are just so complementary in all their programmes," said a second analyst who declined to be identified. "It would be nicely monopolistic in short-range missiles."

Raytheon has been a major player in the consolidation of the defence industry. However it has also built up its commercial business, becoming a leader in the construction and engineering, appliance and commercial aircraft sectors.
In April 1995, it acquired E-Systems for more than $2 billion. A year later it bought Chrysler Corp.'s defence electronics business for $475 million.

Analysts said the sale will probably dilute Texas Instruments' 1997 earnings, but said it gives the company a dynamic profile after years of being one of the more conservative -- and at times uninspiring -- players in the high-tech industry.
Texas Instruments stock gained 75 cents to $67.625, while Raytheon was unchanged at $50, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
